title: It's Not Just Students Who Need to Read Books
author: Geoghegan, B.
summary: The author argues that teachers -- not just students -- need to be active readers, and proposes 'What is the best book you've read this year?' as a litmus-test interview question for prospective teachers. With roughly 54% of US adults reading below a sixth-grade level, and college professors lamenting the reading habits of students in education programs, the concern is not abstract: teachers who rarely read may struggle with the fluency and literacy instruction they are expected to model. Beyond basic competence, the question signals whether a candidate brings intellectual curiosity to the classroom -- a trait the author argues is contagious among students. The author also links book-reading to diversity of thought, and to humility: books require a posture of learning from others, which the best educators carry naturally. The piece is grounded in both data on adult literacy and in personal anecdote -- a library-stocking practice for four children -- that illustrates how reading cultures are transmitted across generations.
points: The question 'What is the best book you read this year?' functions as a diagnostic: a candidate who cannot name one may signal that reading is difficult for them -- a liability for anyone charged with teaching literacy.

54% of US adults read below a 6th-grade level, and teachers at professional development conferences have visibly struggled to read aloud from middle-school texts, making teacher reading fluency a genuine systemic concern.
Intellectual curiosity -- modeled by adults who read broadly -- is contagious; students and colleagues notice when a teacher's learning does not stop at the classroom door.

Books cultivate 'diversity of thought' in ways that narrow professional reading cannot: fiction, biography, and outside-field non-fiction bring ideas and perspectives into a school culture that otherwise remains homogeneous.
The author frames reading not as enrichment for teachers but as professional baseline: someone who does not read voluntarily is unlikely to convey to students why reading matters.
quotes: Unfortunately, it is no longer safe to assume that every applicant with a college degree or teaching credential is highly literate. According to recent data [ ], "About 130 million U.S. adults (54% of those aged 16-74) read below a sixth-grade level".

I once attended a professional development conference for educators where attendees were asked to read passages aloud from a novel written for middle school students. Fluency [ ] is a key component of literacy, and some teachers struggled mightily in this area.

If they haven't read a book in the past year, it could signal that reading is not an easy or pleasurable experience for them, which would raise some concern. In addition to ensuring a highly literate teaching staff, as an administrator, I would want a pool of teachers who were intellectually curious.

That humility and desire to learn will be noticed (and hopefully emulated) by their students and colleagues. The concept of 'diversity' has been abused and perverted in recent years, but 'diversity of thought' is still vital to a healthy educational environment, and books can contribute to creating an atmosphere where it is welcomed and encouraged.

I knew which genre each one preferred and would leave with a pile of fantasy books for my oldest son, mysteries and ghost stories for my second son, a mix of books about animals and sports for my third son, and plenty of mermaid tales and fairy stories for my daughter. Their preferences for what they read independently varied widely, but that variation led to great dinnertime and car-ride conversations where they could share information and stories with each other.

Rather, my goal would be to bring together a team with varied interests and genre preferences. The hope is that they would discuss the books they've read (or hope to read) with their colleagues, share why they enjoyed them, and spur coworkers to pick up a book they otherwise would not have chosen.

As an administrator, I would seek out teachers who have the desire and ability to discuss and grapple with ideas rather than gossip or grumble about individuals in the teacher's lounge. Finally, I would want a teaching staff that valued and appreciated the written word.
